L18: # Import map features from a file
L19: 
L20: You can import map features like lines, shapes, and places to your map from KML files, spreadsheets and other files.
L21: 
L22: ## Import map data to a layer
L23: 
L24: Step 1: Prepare your info
L25: ### Import a file
L26: 
L27: Make sure your info is one of these file types:
L28: 
L29:   * CSV
L30:   * TSV
L31:   * KML
L32:   * KMZ
L33:   * GPX
L34:   * XLSX
L35:   * Google Sheet
L36:   * One or more photos in Google Drive or Google Photos
L37: 
L38: Unzipped KML and KMZ files can be up to 5 MB.
L39: 
L40: CSV files and Google Sheet files both support cite2†WKT geometry format†www.ogc.org .
L41: 
L42: Other files can be up to 40 MB.
L43: 
L44: Unless the file is a photo, the first row should have titles. To import data properly, make sure you have a column with one of the following:
L45:   * Latitude-longitude information
L46:   * Addresses
L47:   * Place names
L48:   * WKT-formatted vector geometry objects
L49: 
L50: Do not import files with more than 2,000 rows. You can import up to 100 photos at a time.
L51: 
L52: CSV or Google Sheets support WKT columns named “WKT.”
L53: 
L54: Step 2: Import info into the map
L55:   1. On your computer, sign in to cite3†My Maps†mymaps.google.com .
L56:   2. Open or create a map.
L57:   3. In the map legend, click Add layer.
L58:   4. Give the new layer a name.
L59:   5. Under the new layer, click Import.
L60:   6. Upload the file or photos that have your info. Then click Select.
L61:     1. If you use WKT objects, click the checkbox for WKT to choose a column to position your placemark.
L62: ## Edit an existing layer
L63: 
L64: You can use MyMaps to reimport your layers with Google Sheets and Comma Separated Values (CSVs). This is helpful if you want to keep the styles you’ve made to your data, and still make any updates.
L65: 
L66: There are a few different options on how to sync and merge layers with Google Sheets and CSVs.
L67: 
L68: Replace all items
L69: You can delete all existing map data in a layer and replace it with map features from a file such as a Google Sheet or CSV file. For instance, you can update layer content with the latest weekly earthquake locations from a sheet and continue to style them by magnitude.
L70:   1. In the layer, click the Overflow menu cite4†Image: More†lh3.googleusercontent.com .
L71:   2. Select Reimport and merge cite5†Image: and then†lh3.googleusercontent.com Reimport cite5†Image: and then†lh3.googleusercontent.com Replace all items.
L72:   3. Choose or upload the file containing the data, then click Select.
L73: 
L74: Tip: If you previously styled map features by a data column, then your style rules will be copied to the replacement data.
L75: 
L76: Update map data in a layer
L77: You can update existing map data in a layer to match the map features from a different file. For example, you can track people across the world as their location is updated in a sheet, without losing their custom icons, photos and videos.
L78:   1. In the layer, click the Overflow menu cite4†Image: More†lh3.googleusercontent.com .
L79:   2. Select Reimport and merge cite5†Image: and then†lh3.googleusercontent.com Reimport cite5†Image: and then†lh3.googleusercontent.com Update matching items.
L80:   3. Choose or upload the file containing the data, then click Select.
L81:   4. Select the column from “Layer data” and the corresponding column from “Uploaded data” to match the features.
L82:   5. Click Finish.
L83: 
L84: Tips:
L85:   * If you previously styled map features by a data column, then your style rules will be copied to the replacement data.
L86:   * Any map features in the original layer that don’t match the new file will be deleted.
L87:   * Any map features in the original layer that match the new file will be preserved including photos or custom styles.
L88:   * Any new map features in the file will be added to your map.
L89: 
L90: Add more items to an existing layer
L91: You can add new map data to an existing layer using a sheet or a CSV. This adds the map data to your existing layer.
L92: 
L93:   1. In the layer, click the Overflow menu cite4†Image: More†lh3.googleusercontent.com .
L94:   2. Select Reimport and merge cite5†Image: and then†lh3.googleusercontent.com Add more items.
L95:   3. Choose or upload the file containing the data, then click Select.
L96: 
L97: Merge matching items
L98: You can also merge data sets based on a matching column in your sheet or CSV. For example, if 2 different files share a column, this column can be used to merge the 2 data sets on the map. You can join a “US states” and an “election result” data set together based on state codes.
L99:   1. To import your first data set, in the layer, click Import.
L100:   2. In the layer, click the Overflow menu cite4†Image: More†lh3.googleusercontent.com .
L101:   3. Select Reimport and merge cite5†Image: and then†lh3.googleusercontent.com Merge matching items.
L102:   4. Choose or upload the second file containing the matching column, then click Select.
L103:   5. Select the column from “Layer data” and the corresponding column from “Uploaded data” to match the features.
L104:   6. Click Finish.
L105: ## Learn about importing or modifying info problems
L106: 
L107: If you can’t import your info correctly:
L108: 
L109:   * Check if the file is in the correct format.
L110:   * Allow `https://mymaps.google.com/` to open your Drive. cite6†Learn how to allow or block content settings for certain sites in Chrome. L111:   * Make sure your column with WKT data is properly labeled as “WKT” only.
L112: 
L113: KML files may not import all their data. The data includes:
L114:   * Info balloons with HTML or JavaScript
L115:   * KML tours
L116:   * Time-based elements
L117:   * Image and screen overlays
L118:   * MultiGeometries
L119:   * 3D models
L120:   * Folders
L121: 
L122: You may have trouble modifying your WKT column after you import it.
L123: 
L124:   * WKT columns are geometries on import. They're no longer text-based.
L125:   * To edit them, you can use the standard geometry editing tools. You can’t edit them in the table editor the same way an address column can.
L126:

L78:     * cite37†Using Cloud Connections L79: As part of an Open Source Software ecosystem, QGIS is built upon different libraries that, combined with its own providers, offer capabilities to read and often write a lot of formats:
L80: 
L81:   * Vector data formats include GeoPackage, GML, GeoJSON, GPX, KML, Comma Separated Values, ESRI formats (Shapefile, Geodatabase…), MapInfo and MicroStation file formats, AutoCAD DWG/DXF, GRASS and many more… Read the complete list of cite38†supported vector formats†gdal.org .
L82:   * Raster data formats include GeoTIFF, JPEG, ASCII Gridded XYZ, MBTiles, R or Idrisi rasters, GDAL Virtual, SRTM, Sentinel Data, ERDAS IMAGINE, ArcInfo Binary Grid, ArcInfo ASCII Grid, and many more… Read the complete list of cite39†supported raster formats†gdal.org .
L83: 
L84:   * Database formats include PostgreSQL, SQLite/SpatiaLite, Oracle, MS SQL Server, SAP HANA, MySQL…
L85:   * Web map and data services (WM(T)S, WFS, WCS, CSW, XYZ tiles, ArcGIS services, …) are also handled by QGIS providers. See cite40†Working with OGC / ISO protocols for more information about some of these.
L86: 
L87:   * You can read supported files from archived folders and use QGIS native formats such as QML files (cite41†QML - The QGIS Style File Format ) and virtual and memory layers.
L88: 
L89: More than 80 vector and 140 raster formats are supported by cite42†GDAL†gdal.org and QGIS native providers.
L90: 
L91: Note
L92: Not all of the listed formats may work in QGIS for various reasons. For example, some require external proprietary libraries, or the GDAL/OGR installation of your OS may not have been built to support the format you want to use. To see the list of available formats, run the command line `ogrinfo --formats` (for vector) and `gdalinfo --formats` (for raster), or check the Settings ► Options ► GDAL menu in QGIS.
L93: In QGIS, depending on the data format, there are different tools to open a dataset, mainly available in the Layer ► Add Layer ► menu or from the Manage Layers toolbar (enabled through View ► Toolbars menu). However, all these tools point to a unique dialog, the Data Source Manager dialog, that you can open with the ^{Open Data Source Manager} button, available on the Data Source Manager Toolbar, or by pressing `Ctrl`+`L`. The Data Source Manager dialog (cite43†Fig.
L94: 11.1 ) offers a unified interface to open file-based data as well as databases or web services supported by QGIS.
L95: cite44†Image: ../../../_images/datasource_manager.png L96: 
L97: Fig. 11.1 QGIS Data Source Manager dialogcite45† L98: 
L99: Beside this main entry point, you also have the DB Manager plugin that offers advanced capabilities to analyze and manipulate connected databases. More information on DB Manager capabilities can be found in cite46†DB Manager Plugin .
L100: 
L101: There are many other tools, native or third-party plugins, that help you open various data formats.
L102: This chapter will describe only the tools provided by default in QGIS for loading data. It will mainly focus on the Data Source Manager dialog but more than describing each tab, it will also explore the tools based on the data provider or format specificities.
L103: ## cite47†11.1.1. The Browser Panel cite3† L104: 
L105: The Browser is one of the main ways to quickly and easily add your data to projects. It’s available as:
L106: 
L107:   * a Data Source Manager tab, enabled pressing the ^{Open Data Source Manager} button (`Ctrl`+`L`);
L108: 
L109:   * as a QGIS panel you can open from the menu View ► Panels (or Settings ► Panels) or by pressing `Ctrl`+`2`.
L110: In both cases, the Browser helps you navigate in your file system and manage geodata, regardless the type of layer (raster, vector, table), or the datasource format (plain or compressed files, databases, web services).
L111: ### cite48†11.1.1.1. Exploring the Interface cite4† L112: 
L113: At the top of the Browser panel, you find some buttons that help you to:
L114: 
L115:   * ^{Add Selected Layers}: you can also add data to the map canvas by selecting Add selected layer(s) from the layer’s context menu;
L116: 
L117:   * ^{Refresh} the browser tree;
L118:   * ^{Filter Browser} to search for specific data. Enter a search word or wildcard and the browser will filter the tree to only show paths to matching DB tables, filenames or folders – other data or folders won’t be displayed. See the Browser Panel(2) example in cite49†Fig. 11.2 . The comparison can be case-sensitive or not. It can also be set to:
L119: 
L120:     * Normal: show items containing the search text
L121:     * Wildcard(s): fine tune the search using the `?` and/or `*` characters to specify the position of the search text
L122: 
L123:     * Regular expression
L124: 
L125:   * ^{Collapse All} the whole tree;
L126: 
L127:   * ^{Enable/disable properties widget}: when toggled on, a new widget is added at the bottom of the panel showing, if applicable, metadata for the selected item.
L128: 
L129: The entries in the Browser panel are organised hierarchically, and there are several top level entries:
L130:   1. Favorites where you can place shortcuts to often used locations
L131: 
L132:   2. Spatial Bookmarks where you can store often used map extents (see cite50†Bookmarking extents on the map )
L133: 
L134:   3. Project Home: for a quick access to the folder in which (most of) the data related to your project are stored. The default value is the directory where your project file resides.
L135: 
L136:   4. Home directory in the file system and the filesystem root directory.
L137: 
L138:   5. Connected local or network drives
L139:   6. Then comes a number of container / database types and service protocols, depending on your platform and underlying libraries:
L140: 
L141:      * GeoPackage
L142: 
L143:      * SpatiaLite
L144: 
L145:      * PostgreSQL
L146: 
L147:      * SAP HANA
L148: 
L149:      * MS SQL Server
L150: 
L151:      * Oracle
L152: 
L153:      * WMS/WMTS
L154: 
L155:      * Vector Tiles
L156: 
L157:      * XYZ Tiles
L158: 
L159:      * WCS
L160: 
L161:      * WFS/OGC API-Features
L162: 
L163:      * ArcGIS REST Server
L164: ### cite51†11.1.1.2. Interacting with the Browser items cite5† L165: 
L166: The browser supports drag and drop within the browser, from the browser to the canvas and Layers panel, and from the Layers panel to layer containers (e.g. GeoPackage) in the browser.
L167: Project file items inside the browser can be expanded, showing the full layer tree (including groups) contained within that project. Project items are treated the same way as any other item in the browser, so they can be dragged and dropped within the browser (for example to copy a layer item to a geopackage file) or added to the current project through drag and drop or double click.
L168: 
L169: The context menu for an element in the Browser panel is opened by right-clicking on it.
L170: For file system directory entries, the context menu offers the following:
L171: 
L172:   * New ► to create in the selected entry a:
L173: 
L174:     * Directory…
L175: 
L176:     * GeoPackage…
L177: 
L178:     * ShapeFile…
L179: 
L180:   * Add as a Favorite: favorite folders can be renamed (Rename favorite…) or removed (Remove favorite) any time.
L181: 
L182:   * Hide from Browser: hidden folders can be toggled to visible from the Settings ► Options ► Data Sources ► Hidden browser paths setting
L183: 
L184:   * Fast Scan this Directory
L185: 
L186:   * Open Directory
L187: 
L188:   * Open in Terminal
L189:   * Properties…
L190: 
L191:   * Directory Properties…
L192: 
L193: For leaf entries that can act as layers in the project, the context menu will have supporting entries. For example, for non-database, non-service-based vector, raster and mesh data sources:
L194: 
L195:   * Export Layer ► To File…
L196: 
L197:   * Add Layer to Project
L198: 
L199:   * Layer Properties
L200: 
L201:   * Open with Data Source Manager…
L202: 
L203:   * Manage ► Rename “<name of file>”… or Delete “<name of file>”…
L204: 
L205:   * Show in Files
L206: 
L207:   * File Properties
L208: In the Layer properties entry, you will find (similar to what you will find in the cite52†vector and cite53†raster layer properties once the layers have been added to the project):
L209: 
L210:   * Metadata for the layer. Metadata groups: Information from provider (if possible, Path will be a hyperlink to the source), Identification, Extent, Access, Fields (for vector layers), Bands (for raster layers), Contacts, Links (for vector layers), References (for raster layers), History.
L211: 
L212:   * A Preview panel
L213:   * The attribute table for vector sources (in the Attributes panel).
L214: 
L215: Use Open with Data Source Manager… to directly open and configure the data source in the Data Source Manager using the URI of your data source. This simplifies the process of adding a layer from the Browser by allowing you to set specific opening options for the data source. It is currently available for vector (including the dedicated GeoPackage entry), raster, and SpatiaLite data sources.
L216: To add a layer to the project using the Browser:
L217: 
L218:   1. Enable the Browser as described above. A browser tree with your file system, databases and web services is displayed. You may need to connect databases and web services before they appear (see dedicated sections).
L219: 
L220:   2. Find the layer in the list.
L221: 
L222:   3. Use the context menu, double-click its name, or drag-and-drop it into the cite54†map canvas . Your layer is now added to the cite55†Layers panel and can be viewed on the map canvas.
L223: 
L224: Tip
L225: Open a QGIS project directly from the browser
L226: 
L227: You can also open a QGIS project directly from the Browser panel by double-clicking its name or by drag-and-drop into the map canvas.
L228: Once a file is loaded, you can zoom around it using the map navigation tools. To change the style of a layer, open the Layer Properties dialog by double-clicking on the layer name or by right-clicking on the name in the legend and choosing Properties from the context menu. See section cite56†Symbology Properties for more information on setting symbology for vector layers.
L229: 
L230: Right-clicking an item in the browser tree helps you to:
L231:   * for a file or a table, display its metadata or open it in your project. Tables can even be renamed, deleted or truncated.
L232: 
L233:   * for a folder, bookmark it into your favourites or hide it from the browser tree. Hidden folders can be managed from the Settings ► Options ► Data Sources tab.
L234: 
L235:   * manage your cite50†spatial bookmarks : bookmarks can be created, exported and imported as `XML` files.
L236: 
L237:   * create a connection to a database or a web service.
L238: 
L239:   * refresh, rename or delete a schema.
L240: You can also import files into databases or copy tables from one schema/database to another with a simple drag-and-drop. There is a second browser panel available to avoid long scrolling while dragging. Just select the file and drag-and-drop from one panel to the other.
L241: 
L242: cite57†Image: ../../../_images/browser_panels.png L243: 
L244: Fig. 11.2 QGIS Browser panels side-by-sidecite58† L245: 
L246: Tip
L247: 
L248: Add layers to QGIS by simple drag-and-drop from your OS file browser
L249: You can also add file(s) to the project by drag-and-dropping them from your operating system file browser to the Layers Panel or the map canvas.
L250: ## cite59†11.1.2. The DB Manager cite6† L251: 
L252: The DB Manager Plugin is another tool for integrating and managing spatial database formats supported by QGIS (PostgreSQL, SpatiaLite, GeoPackage, Oracle Spatial, MS SQL Server, Virtual layers). It can be activated from the Plugins ► Manage and Install Plugins… menu.
L253: 
L254: The ^{DB Manager} Plugin provides several features:
L255: 
L256:   * connect to databases and display their structure and contents
L257: 
L258:   * preview tables of databases
L259:   * add layers to the map canvas, either by double-clicking or drag-and-drop.
L260: 
L261:   * add layers to a database from the QGIS Browser or from another database
L262: 
L263:   * create SQL queries and add their output to the map canvas
L264: 
L265:   * create cite60†virtual layers L266: 
L267: More information on DB Manager capabilities is found in cite46†DB Manager Plugin .
L268: 
L269: cite61†Image: ../../../_images/db_manager.png L270: 
L271: Fig. 11.3 DB Manager dialogcite62† L272: ## cite63†11.1.3. Provider-based loading tools cite7† L273: 
L274: Beside the Browser Panel and the DB Manager, the main tools provided by QGIS to add layers, you’ll also find tools that are specific to data providers.
L275: 
L276: Note
L277: 
L278: Some cite64†external plugins also provide tools to open specific format files in QGIS.
L279: ### cite65†11.1.3.1. Loading a layer from a file cite8† L280: 
L281: To load a layer from a file:
L282: 
L283:   1. Open the layer type tab in the Data Source Manager dialog, ie click the ^{Open Data Source Manager} button (or press `Ctrl`+`L`) and enable the target tab or:
L284: 
L285:      * for vector data (like GML, ESRI Shapefile, Mapinfo and DXF layers): press `Ctrl`+`Shift`+`V`, select the Layer ► Add Layer ► Add Vector Layer menu option or click on the ^{Add Vector Layer} toolbar button.
L286: cite66†Image: ../../../_images/addvectorlayerdialog.png L287: 
L288: Fig. 11.4 Add Vector Layer Dialogcite67† L289: 
L290:      * for raster data (like GeoTiff, MBTiles, GRIdded Binary and DWG layers): press `Ctrl`+`Shift`+`R`, select the Layer ► Add Layer ► Add Raster Layer menu option or click on the ^{Add Raster Layer} toolbar button.
L291: 
L292: cite68†Image: ../../../_images/addrasterlayerdialog.png L293: 
L294: Fig. 11.5 Add Raster Layer Dialogcite69† L295: 
L296:   2. Check File source type
L297: 
L298:   3. Click on the … ^{Browse} button
L299:   4. Navigate the file system and load a supported data source. More than one layer can be loaded at the same time by holding down the `Ctrl` key and clicking on multiple items in the dialog or holding down the `Shift` key to select a range of items by clicking on the first and last items in the range. Only formats that have been well tested appear in the formats filter. Other formats can be loaded by selecting `All files` (the top item in the pull-down menu).
L300:   5. Press Open to load the selected file into Data Source Manager dialog.
L301: 
L302: Depending on the selected layer type, additional Options (encoding, geometry type, table filtering, file locking, data formatting …) are available for configuring. These options are described in detail in the specific GDAL cite70†vector†gdal.org or cite71†raster†gdal.org driver documentation. At the top of the options, a text with hyperlink will directly lead to the documentation of the appropriate driver for the selected file format.
L303: cite72†Image: ../../../_images/openoptionsvectorlayer.png L304: 
L305: Fig. 11.6 Loading a Shapefile with open optionscite73† L306: 
L307:   6. Press Add to load the file in QGIS and display them in the map view. When adding vector datasets containing multiple layers, the Select Items to Add dialog will appear. In this dialog, you can choose the specific layers from your dataset that you want to add. Also, under Options you can choose to:
L308: 
L309:      * Add layers to a group
L310: 
L311:      * Show system and internal tables
L312:      * Show empty vector layers.
L313: 
L314: cite74†Fig. 11.7 shows QGIS after loading the `alaska.shp` file.
L315: 
L316: cite75†Image: ../../../_images/shapefileloaded.png L317: 
L318: Fig. 11.7 QGIS with Shapefile of Alaska loadedcite76† L319: 
L320: Note
L321: 
L322: Because some formats like MapInfo (e.g., `.tab`) or Autocad (`.dxf`) allow mixing different types of geometry in a single file, loading such datasets opens a dialog to select geometries to use in order to have one geometry per layer.
L323: The ^{Add Vector Layer} and ^{Add Raster Layer} tabs allow loading of layers from source types other than File:
L324: 
L325:   * You can load specific vector formats like `ArcInfo Binary Coverage`, `UK. National Transfer Format`, as well as the raw TIGER format of the `US Census Bureau` or `OpenfileGDB`. To do that, you select Directory as Source type. In this case, a directory can be selected in the dialog after pressing … ^{Browse}.
L326:   * With the Database source type you can select an existing database connection or create one to the selected database type. Some possible database types are `ODBC`, `Esri Personal Geodatabase`, `MS SQL Server` as well as `PostgreSQL` or `MySQL` .
L327: 
L328: Pressing the New button opens the Create a New OGR Database Connection dialog whose parameters are among the ones you can find in cite77†Creating a stored Connection . Pressing Open lets you select from the available tables.
L329:   * The Protocol: HTTP(S), cloud, etc. source type opens data stored locally or on the network, either publicly accessible, or in private buckets of commercial cloud storage services. Supported protocol types are:
L330: 
L331:     * `HTTP/HTTPS/FTP`, with a URI and, if required, an cite78†authentication .
L332:     * Cloud storage such as `AWS S3`, `Google Cloud Storage`, `Microsoft Azure Blob`, `Microsoft Azure Data Lake Storage`, `Alibaba OSS Cloud`, and `Open Stack Swift Storage` supports direct control over VSI Credential Options when adding OGR vector or GDAL raster layers. You need to fill in the Bucket or container and the Object key first. After that, you can add the necessary Credential Options.
L333: When adding OGR vector or GDAL raster layers from the cloud based protocols, you can also set additional Credential options for that specific driver and bucket. When credential options are found in a layer’s URI, they will also be automatically set. This allows different layers to use different credentials.
